Verification against the PST package

Written by Mohammed Saqr and Sonsoles López-Pernas

Source: vignettes/articles/verification.Rmd
verification.Rmd

Two questions can be asked of statistical software. Verification asks whether the program computes what its method defines: the counts, the estimates, the likelihood. Validation asks whether the method, as computed, describes the process it is applied to. This article is about the first question for transitiontrees. The package is an independent implementation of the variable-order prediction suffix tree (Ron, Singer and Tishby, 1996), also known as the variable length Markov chain (Bühlmann and Wyner, 1999). Its code shares nothing with the reference implementation of the model in R, the PST package (Gabadinho and Ritschard, 2016), which was archived on CRAN after version 0.94.1.

The verification has two parts. The first runs in this article: on a small bundled dataset, every quantity the tree estimates is computed again by hand with a few lines of base R and compared with the package’s output. The second is an external equivalence suite that fits the same models with PST 0.94.1, the markovchain package and the tna package and compares the results quantity by quantity. The suite lives outside the package, in the source repository, so that neither R CMD check nor a user needs the archived PST package.

What the tree estimates

For a context ss, a sequence of up to max_depth states read oldest to newest, let N(s,a)N(s, a) be the number of times state aa follows ss in the data and N(s)=∑aN(s,a)N(s) = \sum_a N(s, a). Every position of every sequence is counted once for the root and once for each preceding run of states up to max_depth, so the first state of a sequence is counted only at the root and the second at the root and at depth one. A context enters the tree when N(s)≥N(s) \gemin_count. Its maximum-likelihood next-state distribution is

P̂(a∣s)=N(s,a)/N(s).\hat P(a \mid s) = N(s, a) / N(s).

The default floor smoother changes only a distribution in which some state has a zero count. With kk states and floor yy (ymin), it becomes

P̃(a∣s)=(1−ky)P̂(a∣s)+y,\tilde P(a \mid s) = (1 - k\,y)\,\hat P(a \mid s) + y,

which is the rule used by PST. To predict a position, the tree uses the longest context it holds among the states that precede it, and the log-likelihood of a set of sequences is the sum, over all positions, of the log-probability the tree gives to the observed state.

Data

The hand computation uses the first ten learners of trajectories.

  • Sequence: one row per learner.
  • Time: columns 1 to 15; trailing NAs mark the end of a shorter trajectory.
  • State: Active, Average or Disengaged.
library(transitiontrees)
learners <- head(trajectories, 10)

Counting by hand

The hand computation needs two small functions written in base R, which use nothing from the package. count_by_hand() lists, for every position of every sequence, the root and each preceding run of up to max_depth states, and tabulates the state that follows. It returns one row per context with its total count and its count of each next state. contexts_of() turns the pathway names of that table into histories that can be passed to predict().

count_by_hand <- function(sequences, max_depth) {
  events <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(sequences)), function(i) {
    states <- unname(sequences[i, ])
    states <- states[!is.na(states)]
    per_depth <- lapply(seq.int(0L, max_depth), function(d) {
      positions <- seq_along(states)
      positions <- positions[positions > d]
      pathway <- vapply(positions, function(t) {
        if (d == 0L) "(start)" else
          paste(states[seq.int(t - d, t - 1L)], collapse = " -> ")
      }, character(1))
      data.frame(pathway = pathway, next_state = states[positions])
    })
    do.call(rbind, per_depth)
  })
  events <- do.call(rbind, events)
  counts <- table(events$pathway, events$next_state)
  data.frame(pathway = rownames(counts),
             count = as.integer(rowSums(counts)),
             as.data.frame.matrix(counts), row.names = NULL)
}

contexts_of <- function(hand) {
  lapply(hand$pathway, function(p) {
    if (identical(p, "(start)")) character(0) else
      strsplit(p, " -> ", fixed = TRUE)[[1L]]
  })
}

To count the contexts up to depth two, we call count_by_hand().

hand <- count_by_hand(learners, max_depth = 2L)
hand
#>                     pathway count Active Average Disengaged
#> 1                   (start)   147     64      68         15
#> 2                    Active    60     43      15          2
#> 3          Active -> Active    40     32       7          1
#> 4         Active -> Average    14      8       6          0
#> 5      Active -> Disengaged     2      1       0          1
#> 6                   Average    62     13      41          8
#> 7         Average -> Active    12      5       7          0
#> 8        Average -> Average    36      4      28          4
#> 9     Average -> Disengaged     8      0       6          2
#> 10               Disengaged    15      3       7          5

The ten learners contribute 147 observed states, all counted at the root. All nine pairs of states occur as contexts of depth two, so the hand count has 13 contexts.

Counts

To fit the tree that keeps every observed context, we call context_tree() with min_count = 1L; smoothing = list("floor", ymin = 0) switches the smoother off so that the probabilities are the raw maximum-likelihood estimates.

tree <- context_tree(learners, max_depth = 2L, min_count = 1L,
                     smoothing = list("floor", ymin = 0))
tree
#> <transitiontrees>  13 nodes, depth <= 2, 3 states  [unpruned]
#>   alphabet : Active, Average, Disengaged
#>   fit on   : 10 sequences, 147 observations
#>   smoothing: floor(ymin=0, rule=interpolate)   min_count = 1
#> (start)   n=147    -> Average (0.46)
#> |-- Active    n=60     -> Active (0.72)
#> |   |-- Active    n=40     -> Active (0.80)
#> |   |-- Average   n=12     -> Average (0.58)
#> |   `-- Disengaged  n=3      -> Active (1.00)
#> |-- Average   n=62     -> Average (0.66)
#> |   |-- Active    n=14     -> Active (0.57)
#> |   |-- Average   n=36     -> Average (0.78)
#> |   `-- Disengaged  n=7      -> Average (0.57)
#> `-- Disengaged  n=15     -> Average (0.47)
#>     |-- Active    n=2      -> Active (0.50)
#>     |-- Average   n=8      -> Average (0.75)
#>     `-- Disengaged  n=5      -> Active (0.40)

To compare the counts, we merge the hand table with the tree’s table from as.data.frame() by pathway.

counts <- merge(subset(hand, select = c(pathway, count)),
                subset(as.data.frame(tree), select = c(pathway, count)),
                by = "pathway", suffixes = c("_hand", "_tree"))
counts
#>                     pathway count_hand count_tree
#> 1                   (start)        147        147
#> 2                    Active         60         60
#> 3          Active -> Active         40         40
#> 4         Active -> Average         14         14
#> 5      Active -> Disengaged          2          2
#> 6                   Average         62         62
#> 7         Average -> Active         12         12
#> 8        Average -> Average         36         36
#> 9     Average -> Disengaged          8          8
#> 10               Disengaged         15         15
#> 11     Disengaged -> Active          3          3
#> 12    Disengaged -> Average          7          7
#> 13 Disengaged -> Disengaged          5          5
c(by_hand = nrow(hand), in_tree = n_nodes(tree), matched = nrow(counts))
#> by_hand in_tree matched 
#>      13      13      13
with(counts, identical(count_hand, count_tree))
#> [1] TRUE

The tree holds the same 13 contexts as the hand count, and every count is identical. The number of observations the tree reports, nobs(), equals the root count.

nobs(tree)
#> [1] 147

Maximum-likelihood probabilities

To compute the maximum-likelihood distributions by hand, we divide each next state’s count by the context’s count. To obtain the tree’s distributions, we call predict() with each context as a history and tidy = TRUE.

mle_by_hand <- function(hand) {
  states <- setdiff(names(hand), c("pathway", "count"))
  data.frame(pathway = hand$pathway, hand[states] / hand$count)
}
by_hand <- mle_by_hand(hand)
fitted <- predict(tree, newdata = contexts_of(hand), tidy = TRUE)
subset(fitted, select = c(history, context, Active, Average, Disengaged))
#>                     history                  context Active Average Disengaged
#> 1                   (start)                  (start) 0.4354  0.4626    0.10204
#> 2                    Active                   Active 0.7167  0.2500    0.03333
#> 3          Active -> Active         Active -> Active 0.8000  0.1750    0.02500
#> 4         Active -> Average        Active -> Average 0.5714  0.4286    0.00000
#> 5      Active -> Disengaged     Active -> Disengaged 0.5000  0.0000    0.50000
#> 6                   Average                  Average 0.2097  0.6613    0.12903
#> 7         Average -> Active        Average -> Active 0.4167  0.5833    0.00000
#> 8        Average -> Average       Average -> Average 0.1111  0.7778    0.11111
#> 9     Average -> Disengaged    Average -> Disengaged 0.0000  0.7500    0.25000
#> 10               Disengaged               Disengaged 0.2000  0.4667    0.33333
#> 11     Disengaged -> Active     Disengaged -> Active 1.0000  0.0000    0.00000
#> 12    Disengaged -> Average    Disengaged -> Average 0.0000  0.5714    0.42857
#> 13 Disengaged -> Disengaged Disengaged -> Disengaged 0.4000  0.2000    0.40000
identical(with(fitted, context), with(by_hand, pathway))
#> [1] TRUE
all.equal(subset(fitted, select = c(Active, Average, Disengaged)),
          subset(by_hand, select = c(Active, Average, Disengaged)),
          tolerance = 1e-12)
#> [1] TRUE

Every history is predicted from its own context, without back-off, and the probabilities agree with the hand computation to within 10−1210^{-12}.

Floor smoothing

Six of the hand-counted distributions contain a zero, for example Active -> Disengaged (one Active, one Disengaged, no Average). To check the default smoother, we apply the floor rule by hand with ymin = 0.001 and compare it with a tree fitted with the default smoothing.

floor_by_hand <- function(probabilities, ymin) {
  states <- setdiff(names(probabilities), "pathway")
  p <- as.matrix(probabilities[states])
  k <- length(states)
  has_zero <- rowSums(p == 0) > 0
  p[has_zero, ] <- (1 - k * ymin) * p[has_zero, ] + ymin
  data.frame(pathway = probabilities$pathway, p)
}
smoothed_tree <- context_tree(learners, max_depth = 2L, min_count = 1L)
smoothed <- predict(smoothed_tree, newdata = contexts_of(hand), tidy = TRUE)
all.equal(subset(smoothed, select = c(Active, Average, Disengaged)),
          subset(floor_by_hand(by_hand, ymin = 0.001),
                 select = c(Active, Average, Disengaged)),
          tolerance = 1e-12)
#> [1] TRUE

The log-likelihood

To compute the log-likelihood by hand, we score every position with the hand-computed distribution of its longest preceding context and sum the logarithms.

loglik_by_hand <- function(sequences, max_depth, probabilities) {
  states_all <- setdiff(names(probabilities), "pathway")
  p <- as.matrix(probabilities[states_all])
  rownames(p) <- probabilities$pathway
  per_sequence <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(sequences)), function(i) {
    states <- unname(sequences[i, ])
    states <- states[!is.na(states)]
    sum(vapply(seq_along(states), function(t) {
      d <- min(t - 1L, max_depth)
      context <- if (d == 0L) "(start)" else
        paste(states[seq.int(t - d, t - 1L)], collapse = " -> ")
      log(p[context, states[t]])
    }, numeric(1)))
  }, numeric(1))
  sum(per_sequence)
}
loglik_by_hand(learners, max_depth = 2L, probabilities = by_hand)
#> [1] -99.95
logLik(tree)
#> 'log Lik.' -99.95 (df=26)
all.equal(loglik_by_hand(learners, max_depth = 2L, probabilities = by_hand),
          as.numeric(logLik(tree)), tolerance = 1e-12)
#> [1] TRUE

The same check on the full data

The same comparison can be run on all the bundled sequences at several depths. verify_by_hand() combines the steps above and returns one row per dataset and depth: the number of contexts found by hand and in the tree, and the largest absolute differences in counts, probabilities and log-likelihood.

verify_by_hand <- function(sequences, max_depth, label) {
  hand <- count_by_hand(sequences, max_depth)
  tree <- context_tree(sequences, max_depth = max_depth, min_count = 1L,
                       smoothing = list("floor", ymin = 0))
  tree_counts <- as.data.frame(tree)
  matched <- merge(hand, tree_counts, by = "pathway",
                   suffixes = c("_hand", "_tree"))
  by_hand <- mle_by_hand(hand)
  states <- setdiff(names(by_hand), "pathway")
  fitted <- predict(tree, newdata = contexts_of(hand), tidy = TRUE)
  data.frame(
    data = label, max_depth = max_depth,
    contexts_hand = nrow(hand), contexts_tree = n_nodes(tree),
    max_count_error = max(abs(matched$count_hand - matched$count_tree)),
    max_prob_error = max(abs(as.matrix(fitted[states]) -
                               as.matrix(by_hand[states]))),
    loglik_error = abs(loglik_by_hand(sequences, max_depth, by_hand) -
                         as.numeric(logLik(tree))))
}
checks <- Map(verify_by_hand,
              sequences = list(trajectories, trajectories, trajectories,
                               as.matrix(engagement), as.matrix(engagement)),
              max_depth = c(1L, 2L, 3L, 1L, 2L),
              label = c("trajectories", "trajectories", "trajectories",
                        "engagement", "engagement"))
do.call(rbind, checks)
#>           data max_depth contexts_hand contexts_tree max_count_error max_prob_error loglik_error
#> 1 trajectories         1             4             4               0              0    0.000e+00
#> 2 trajectories         2            13            13               0              0    2.274e-13
#> 3 trajectories         3            40            40               0              0    0.000e+00
#> 4   engagement         1             4             4               0              0    0.000e+00
#> 5   engagement         2            13            13               0              0    1.819e-12

On the 136 non-empty trajectories and the 1,000 engagement sequences, at every depth, the tree holds exactly the contexts found by hand, the counts and the probabilities are identical, and the log-likelihoods differ by at most 2×10−112 \times 10^{-11}, the rounding error of summing thousands of logarithms in a different order. (as.matrix() gives the engagement data frame the same matrix form as trajectories, which the hand-count function expects.)

The external equivalence suite

The hand computation verifies the estimator against its definition. The external suite verifies it against implementations written by other authors. It is kept in local_testing_and_equivalence/ in the source repository, outside the built package, and runs only when the environment variable TRANSITREES_EQUIV_TESTS is true. Its runner installs PST 0.94.1 from the CRAN archive, installs the current source of transitiontrees, and runs three test files.

PST. Thirty configurations are drawn at random with a fixed seed. Each simulates first-order Markov sequences from a random transition matrix with 2 to 4 states, 50, 80 or 120 sequences of length 15, 20 or 25, and fits both packages with max_depth from 2 to 4, min_count (nmin in PST) of 3, 5 or 8, and ymin of 0, 0.001 or 0.005. TraMineR builds the sequence object that PST requires. Every configuration is compared on:

transitiontrees PST 0.94.1 Criterion
node counts, all depths (context_tree()) pstree() node counts identical integers
node probabilities, all depths pstree() node probabilities absolute difference < 10−1010^{-10}
set of contexts nodenames() identical sets
nobs() nobs() identical
query_pathway() query() absolute difference < 10−1010^{-10}
per-position probabilities (score_positions()) predict(decomp = TRUE) absolute difference < 10−910^{-9}
logLik() logLik() relative difference < 10−1010^{-10}
plot_pruning() distributions and counts query() and node counts < 10−1010^{-10}; identical
plot_predictive(type = "logloss") −log⁡2-\log_2 of predict(decomp = TRUE) absolute difference < 10−910^{-9}
prune_tree(criterion = "G2") prune(gain = "G2") measured agreement (below)

markovchain. A tree of depth one without smoothing is a first-order Markov chain. Its transition probabilities are compared with the maximum-likelihood estimate of markovchain::markovchainFit() on three simulated datasets with 2, 3 and 4 states (absolute difference < 10−1210^{-12}).

tna. prepare_input(), which turns a long event log into sequences, is compared with tna::prepare_data() over every combination of its arguments (actor, time, order, action and the session time threshold) on three long-format datasets from the Nestimate package, and an explicit session column is checked to split sequences by actor and session.

Results

The suites were last run on 2026-11-17 against transitiontrees 0.1.5 on R 4.5.2 (Linux), with PST 0.94.1 installed from the CRAN archive, markovchain from CRAN and tna 1.5.8.

Suite Tests (expectations) Failures Max abs count error Max abs probability error
PST 0.94.1 10 (296) 0 0 0 (log-loss: 4.4e-16)
markovchain 1 (1) 0 not applicable 0
tna 2 (422) 0 not applicable not applicable

The PST suite fits 30 random configurations (2 to 4 states, depth 2 to 4, min_count of 3, 5 or 8 and ymin of 0, 0.001 or 0.005). Every shared context has the same counts and probabilities, and the per-position predictive probabilities agree exactly; the only non-zero difference is a log-loss difference of 4.4e-16, at the level of floating-point rounding. For the tna comparison the contract is that both functions produce the same set of sequences for each of the 420 argument combinations. Since tna 1.3.1, sessions built from a time column are ordered numerically by actor, while prepare_input() orders them as text, so the rows agree in order for 153 of the 420 combinations and as a set for all of them. Row order does not change a fitted tree.

What is not at parity

Some functions implement the package’s own design and have no counterpart in PST, so they are verified by the package’s unit tests only.

  • Pruning. prune_tree(criterion = "G2") and PST’s prune(gain = "G2") use the same likelihood-ratio statistic but differ in two documented ways. transitiontrees compares G2G^2 with the chi-square critical value on k−1k - 1 degrees of freedom; PST’s worked example uses a cutoff equivalent to one degree of freedom. transitiontrees computes G2G^2 from the empirical child distribution, PST from the smoothed one, a difference of the order of ymin that can change a decision exactly at the cutoff. The suite measures the consequence: with PST’s one-degree-of-freedom cutoff, the contexts transitiontrees keeps are always a subset of those PST keeps, and the two sets are identical when there are two states; with the cutoff matched to k−1k - 1 degrees of freedom, the kept sets are identical in at least 85% of configurations, the remainder being decisions at the cutoff.
  • Distances, tuning and generation. tree_distance() is a count-weighted symmetric Kullback-Leibler divergence, a different quantity from PST’s distance. tune_tree() uses sequence-level k-fold cross-validation with its own fold assignment. generate_sequences() and simulate() consume random numbers differently from PST, so they can be compared in distribution only.
  • Smoothers. The laplace, kneser_ney, witten_bell and jelinek_mercer smoothers have no PST counterpart. The floor smoother matches PST by default; smoothing = list("floor", ymin = 0.001, rule = "cap") selects the package’s earlier clamp-and-renormalise rule, which differs from PST only at contexts with a zero count, by an amount of the order of ymin.
  • Reshaping. prepare_input() produces the same set of sequences as tna::prepare_data(); their order can differ because the two functions sort session identifiers differently. Row order does not affect the fit.

Running the suite

From the root of the source repository, with PST and the other reference packages available, the suite runs with

TRANSITREES_EQUIV_TESTS=true Rscript local_testing_and_equivalence/run-equiv.R

which installs the reference packages that are missing (PST from the CRAN archive), installs the package from source and prints one row per test with its number of expectations, failures and errors.

References

Bühlmann, P., & Wyner, A. J. (1999). Variable length Markov chains. The Annals of Statistics, 27(2), 480-513. https://doi.org/10.1214/aos/1018031204

Gabadinho, A., & Ritschard, G. (2016). Analyzing state sequences with probabilistic suffix trees: The PST R package. Journal of Statistical Software, 72(3). https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v072.i03

Ron, D., Singer, Y., & Tishby, N. (1996). The power of amnesia: Learning probabilistic automata with variable memory length. Machine Learning, 25(2-3), 117-149. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1026490906255
